title: The Birth Goddesses and the First Families
sum: The fourteen pieces of clay of the last chapter become people, and the poem turns to the rules of human life. Mami, the mother goddess, here also called Nintu and Dingirmah, lays down how births will happen from now on: a brick laid in the house for nine days (seven in the late Nineveh copy), the midwife rejoicing, the mother keeping apart with her baby. Then she speaks of growing up and marriage: boys become young men, girls young women, they look at each other and choose a husband or wife, and Ishtar rejoices for nine days.

In the middle stands the first birth. The birth goddesses gather, Nintu counts the months, and in the tenth month the goddess opens the womb, covers her head, ties her belt, blesses, draws with flour and sets down the brick, crying "I created! My own hands made it!" After a long break the poem shows the new people at work: they make hoes and spades, the tools the gods burned in their strike, and build dikes to feed themselves and the gods.
readings: Read as a charter for family life

For its first hearers the chapter explained why things are done as they are: why a brick is laid at a birth, why the midwife and the holy woman have their place, why weddings last nine days. Each custom is traced back to the goddess who made the first people.

Genesis also moves from the making of humankind to marriage (Genesis 1:27-28; 2:24) and to work (Genesis 2:15). But in Genesis there is one Maker, and the man and woman are given to each other, not decreed by a goddess so that the gods' workers will keep coming.

views.C: A Christian reader finds much that is familiar: male and female, marriage, joy at a birth, the hard work of feeding a household. What is missing is the Giver. Mami claims, "My own hands made it" (4:35), but she works with borrowed clay and the blood of a slain god. In the Bible God says, "My own hands stretched out the heavens" (Isaiah 45:12), and he opens and shuts the womb himself (Genesis 29:31; 30:22). Marriage is his gift from the beginning (Matthew 19:4-6), and children are his reward (Psalm 127:3), not a supply of laborers.
views.H: Copy A breaks off from about line 252 to 280, so the first part of the chapter rests on the Old Babylonian copy E and two Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh, which do not always agree (4:6). Scholars differ on many readings: who takes whose charm (4:16), whether the couples "choose" or "will choose" (4:22), whether the goddess praises Kesh or lays a reed mat (4:46). SEAL's edition settles several of these against Lambert and Millard (1969).
views.M: Babylonian births were in the care of goddesses: the mother goddess and her helpers, the birth goddesses. The midwife's rituals, the birth brick, the flour, the head covering and the blessing, were things the first hearers saw done. The qadištu, a woman set apart for temple service, had a part at births (4:36). Weddings were feasts of Ishtar, goddess of love (4:50-52).
views.S: A spiritual reading notes that the poem gives the honor of birth to a goddess. The Bible warns against giving God's glory to another (Isaiah 42:8) and names the Queen of Heaven, whom many scholars identify with Ishtar, among the gods Judah wrongly served (Jeremiah 7:18; 44:17). Christians who see real powers behind the gods of the nations read Mami's boast as a creature taking the Creator's place (Romans 1:25).
views.J: Jewish writers before Jesus told where human crafts came from in a darker way. In 1 Enoch a fallen angel, Azazel, "taught people to make swords, knives, shields and breastplates" and showed them the metals (1 Enoch 8:1). In Atrahasis the new people make their own hoes and spades to do the gods' work (4:67). Genesis gives the first toolmaker a human name, Tubal-cain (Genesis 4:22).

deep.b: The rules for births appear twice. The first time (4:6-11) only in the Neo-Assyrian copy S+T+, the second (4:36-41) in the Old Babylonian copies A and E, with a Nineveh fragment. They match line by line, with three changes that SEAL's editors trace to a later scribe: "the house of the holy woman" became "the house of the woman in labor," an old verb for the mother's time apart was replaced, and the brick lies seven days instead of nine. The changes show the poem living on for a thousand years, copied by scribes who did not always understand the old words.

deep.title: Clay, brick and the potter
deep.b: My own observation. The chapter is full of clay: the people are formed from clay (3:96; 4:3), births happen over a clay brick (4:7, 4:34, 4:40), and the tablet itself is clay. The Bible uses the same material for a very different picture: God is the potter and we are his clay (Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 18:6), and Paul says that we hold a treasure "in clay pots" (2 Corinthians 4:7). In Atrahasis clay is the goddess's craft; in the Bible it is a sign that the creature belongs to the Maker.

settings.why: To claim the making of humankind ("My own hands made it!") and to set up the customs of birth and marriage in her honor and Ishtar's: nine days for the brick, nine days of joy at a wedding.
settings.readers: Scribes and their pupils in Old Babylonian Sippar: the best copy (A) was written by the junior scribe Ipiq-Aya in the reign of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon, about 1630 BC by Millard's dating (5:87-91). A thousand years later Assyrian scribes copied it again for Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (copies P(+)R(+)KB, S+T+, Q, V).

title: The Noise of Humankind and the Plague
sum: Six hundred years pass, and people fill the land. Their noise roars like a bull, and Enlil, ruler of the earth, cannot sleep. He calls the gods together and orders a plague: chills, sickness and the demon Asakku blow over the people like a storm, and Namtar, whose name means "fate," cuts off their noise.

Now the hero appears. Atrahasis, whose god is Enki and whose ear is open, tells his god that humankind is groaning and blaming the gods. Enki gives a crafty answer: let the heralds tell everyone to stop worshiping their own gods and bring all their offerings to Namtar's door, until the gifts shame him into ending the plague. The elders obey, build Namtar a house, the plague lifts, and health returns. Then the noise comes back as before. The tablet ends with the catch-line "Not yet 1,200 years had passed" and the scribe Ipiq-Aya's note.
readings: For the poem the problem is too many people and too much noise. Anne Kilmer and William Moran argued that the gods are fighting overpopulation (as Frymer-Kensky reports). The plague, the drought and finally the Flood are three tries at one solution.

Genesis also begins its Flood story with people growing many (Genesis 6:1). But it names a different cause: "every plan their hearts shaped was nothing but evil all day long" and "the earth was full of violence" (Genesis 6:5, 11). Millard thought the idea of humankind disturbing God was common to both; the difference is between a god disturbed by noise and the LORD grieved by sin (Genesis 6:6).

views.C: The chapter is a picture of what the world would be with many gods and no Father. The god who rules the earth wants humankind quiet; the god who loves them can only help by trickery; the plague god can be bribed. The Bible's God is one, so judgment and mercy come from the same heart (Hosea 6:1). He "does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4); he hears groaning and remembers his covenant (Exodus 2:24); "he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Atrahasis is saved by a clever god's advice; Noah by grace and faith (Genesis 6:8; Hebrews 11:7).
views.H: Copy A is the base text but is broken at many points, so lines come from the Nineveh copies S+T+, V and Q and the Late Babylonian copies z and bd, with SEAL's restorations from Tablet II. Scholars disagree on the meaning of "noise" (overpopulation, rebellion, or something like the crying of babies) and on several hard words (5:13, 5:36, 5:47). Millard (1967) noted that the 1,200 years have been compared with Genesis 6:3.
views.M: Each Babylonian family served a personal god and goddess, who spoke for it among the great gods. Enki's plan works through that system: if every family stops serving its own gods and serves Namtar alone, Namtar is shamed by the flood of gifts. Offerings of bread and flour were brought to a god's door, and a god accepted them with a gesture of the hand (SEAL). Public orders went out by heralds.
views.S: Christian readers have three ways to read Namtar and the gods of this chapter: as nothing, idols with no power (Psalm 115:4-7); as demons who receive the sacrifices (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20); or as rebel members of God's heavenly council (Psalm 82). All agree that bribing a power to lift a plague is not prayer to the living God, who heals when his people turn to him (2 Chronicles 7:14).
views.J: Jewish writings before Jesus tell the time before the Flood from the side of the sufferers. In 1 Enoch the cries of people killed by the giants rise to heaven, and the angels bring their case to the Most High (1 Enoch 8:4; 9:2-3), who sends word to Noah to hide (1 Enoch 10:1-3). There the human outcry is heard; in Atrahasis it is the problem.

deep.b: Atrahasis and Genesis 6 share an order of events: people multiply, heaven takes notice, a limit is set, and in the end a flood comes. Millard (1967) granted that "din" is not "violence," but thought "the basic idea of disturbing deity is surely common to both narratives," and that Genesis 6:1-4 belongs to a scheme also found in Atrahasis. The differences are the heart of the matter. (1) In Genesis growth is a blessing (1:28) and evil is the problem (6:5, 6:11); in Atrahasis growth itself is the problem. (2) In Genesis heaven's response is grief (6:6); in Atrahasis it is lost sleep. (3) Genesis has no plague, drought or famine before the Flood, only a time limit (6:3). (4) In Genesis the one God both judges and warns; in Atrahasis one god attacks and another undermines him.

The tablet ends with the scribe's note (5:85-91): "Tablet one of 'When the gods were man.' Its lines: 416." Ipiq-Aya, a junior scribe, signed it on the 21st of Nisan, in a year of King Ammi-saduqa of Babylon, which SEAL identifies as his twelfth. The second tablet bears the same scribe's name. Such notes let us name the first readers of the poem: a scribal school in Sippar, copying the classics.

title: The Drought
sum: Twelve hundred years pass and the same thing happens: the land grows wide, the people grow many, their noise keeps Enlil awake. "Did you lay a doom on them?" he asks the gods; "they are more than before!" This time he orders a drought. Adad must keep back his rain, the waters below must not rise, the clouds must gather but drop nothing, and Nisaba, the grain goddess, must shut her breast. The fields turn white with salt, the earth turns back her womb, and the wombs of women are tied shut.

Every order is carried out in the same words. After a broken column, a separate Old Babylonian tablet shows the result: blood clotted, bellies swollen, minds failing, animals unable to eat, and humankind's noise turned to weeping. In those days the sage Atrahasis saw it and went to speak to his lord Enki.
readings: The chapter is built to echo chapter 5 word for word. The repetition is the point: the gods' plan does not work, because people keep growing. Each round is harder than the last.

The Bible also tells of rain withheld, but as a word from God to his people: the covenant warnings (Deuteronomy 11:17; 28:23-24), Elijah's drought against Baal (1 Kings 17:1), and Amos's list of plagues that were meant to bring Israel back (Amos 4:6-11).

views.C: A Christian reads this chapter with the God who "sends rain on righteous and unrighteous people" (Matthew 5:45) in mind. In the Bible drought can be judgment, but it always has a reason, a warning and a way back (1 Kings 8:35-36; 2 Chronicles 7:13-14), and God's settled will is the blessing of fruitful fields and wombs (Genesis 8:22; 9:1). Enlil's drought aims at fewer people; the LORD's droughts aim at repentance and end in rain (James 5:17-18).
views.H: Tablet II is less complete than Tablet I. SEAL arranges it in segments: A from the Old Babylonian copies B and D with the Nineveh copies Q and S+T+; B only from S+T+; C, one column of copy I, placed tentatively; D, the Schøyen tablet MS 2950, edited by Andrew George, with no parallel in any other copy. The later copies often add "above" and "below" and change verbs (6:13-14, 6:21).
views.M: The first hearers lived by irrigation and rain. Adad, the storm god, sent rain; the yearly rise of the Tigris and Euphrates and the springs below fed the canals; Nisaba was grain itself. Salt in the fields was a real fear in southern Babylonia. A drought ordered by the gods' king was the worst disaster imaginable.
views.S: Christian readers see in Adad a form of the storm god Hadad, the Baal whom Elijah faced on Carmel (1 Kings 18). The Bible's answer is that rain belongs to the LORD (Jeremiah 5:24; Job 38:28), whatever power the nations credited. Those who read the gods of the nations as demons (1 Corinthians 10:20) see in Enlil's drought a picture of powers that hate human life; the God of Israel says, "Be fruitful, grow many" (Genesis 9:1).
views.J: Jewish writers before Jesus linked droughts and failing crops with the last days and the sins of the world: in 1 Enoch's book of the heavens, "The rain will be held back, / and the sky will stand still" in the days of sinners (1 Enoch 80:2). There, as in the Bible, the cause is sin; in Atrahasis it is numbers.

deep.b: The drought decree moves from the sky to the field to the womb. The plain "gives birth" to salt (6:27), the earth "turns back her womb" (6:28), and the curse ends, "Let the womb be tied shut" (6:31). The Akkadian word for womb, rēmu, also means compassion, as Hebrew rechem and rachamim do. When Enlil shuts the earth's womb he shuts its mercy. Genesis also binds ground and birth together under one sentence after the first sin (Genesis 3:16-19), but it adds a promise (3:15), and after the Flood God blesses the womb again (9:1, 9:7). The poem's own ending will go the other way, making childlessness and infant death part of the order of the world.

deep.title: Pharaoh as a second Enlil
deep.b: My own comparison (see the note at 6:8). Exodus 1 tells of a ruler alarmed that a people "grew many" (Exodus 1:7), who tries forced labor, then a plan at the births, and fails because God blesses them and the midwives fear God. Atrahasis tells of a divine ruler alarmed at the same thing, who tries plague, drought and famine, and fails until the Flood. If the Israelites knew such stories, Exodus would read as an answer: the power that wants fewer people is the enemy, and the God of Israel is on the side of birth.
